why_angle: The cited TechGearLab review gives the MegaVolt16 Air's measured 51.3 Wh and says it can inflate and still jump. Neither it nor any other rival page gives the makers' rule: WOLFBOX's manual says keep the charge above 50% before a jump, and GOOLOO's guide says at least 2 of 4 bars. Without that rule, nobody works out how much of the shared battery the compressor can use, so this page gives that figure for each model.

page.title: Car Jump Starter with Air Compressor: Keep Half the Battery for the Jump
page.h1: Car jump starter with air compressor: how much battery the pump can use before the jump suffers
page.desc: In a jump starter with an air compressor, one battery runs both. WOLFBOX and GOOLOO say keep about half for jumping. Pump budget, maker prices and tests compared.
page.answer: Short answer. A car jump starter with air compressor runs the clamps and the tire pump off one battery, and both makers want half a charge kept for a jump. The best tested pick, the WOLFBOX MegaVolt16 Air, leaves about 25.7 Wh for the compressor: half of the 51.3 Wh TechGearLab measured.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Pump budget, MegaVolt16 Air: 51.3 Wh measured × 50% ≈ 25.7 Wh above the jump line. On the 59.2 Wh rating it would be 29.6 Wh.
  • Pump budget, MegaVolt 24Air: 88.8 Wh × 50% = 44.4 Wh. Comparing rated figures, that is 44.4 ÷ 29.6 = 1.5 times the 16 Air's budget, for $98.86 more ($278.26 − $179.40).
  • Cost per measured Wh, MegaVolt16 Air: $179.40 ÷ 51.3 Wh = $3.50. TechGearLab's measured 51.3 Wh is 87% of the rated 59.2 Wh (51.3 ÷ 59.2), so the box figure overstates what you get.
  • Inflation pace: TechGearLab measured the 16 Air adding 5 PSI in 3 min to a 275/70 R18 F-150 tire, about 1.7 PSI/min. WOLFBOX's own 24Air claim (30→36 PSI in 1 min 20 s on a 275/70 R17) works out to 6 ÷ 1.33 ≈ 4.5 PSI/min. GOOLOO's A3 claim (0→36 PSI in under 7 min on a 205/55 R16) works out to about 5.1 PSI/min from flat. The makers each use a different tire and pressure range, so only TechGearLab's figure is an independent measurement.
  • Same name, different unit: gooloo.com sells the A3 at $69.99. The A3 Pro is a separate $89.99 listing, $20 more.
  • Peak amps: TechGearLab notes there is no industry standard for measuring peak amps. Use the maker's engine rating as the guide: A3 up to 9.0 L gas / 6.5 L diesel, MegaVolt16 Air 8 L gas / 6 L diesel (TechGearLab), MegaVolt 24Air 10 L gas / 10 L diesel.

One battery, two jobs: why half the charge is spoken for

In a jump starter with an air compressor, the compressor and the clamps draw from the same pack. WOLFBOX's MegaVolt16 Air manual, which also covers the MegaVolt 24 Air, heads its jump-start section “Ensure Battery Level >50%”. GOOLOO's A3 guide says not to jump-start a vehicle if the battery is below 2 of its 4 bars. It also says to make no more than 3 jump attempts in a row, wait 2 minutes between them, and let the unit cool for 30 minutes before recharging. So the half above that line is the compressor's budget, and any tire you inflate beyond it uses charge you need for the jump. If you need both at the roadside, jump the car first while the pack is above the line, then inflate the tires.

Cold weather limits recharging, not jumping. The WOLFBOX manual blocks charging below 0 °C and allows it again only above 5 °C. A pack drained by inflating in freezing weather cannot be topped back up until it warms. WOLFBOX's own how-to guide says to check the display for remaining charge before a jump and to watch the battery when airing up more than one or two tires in a row.

If you inflate often, two batteries avoid the trade-off. A separate cordless inflator such as the {buy:fanttik-x8-apex-tire-inflator} ($59.99 at fanttik.com today) leaves your jump pack full. Fanttik's own Potent T10 1800 A jump starter is $99.99, so the pair costs $159.98.

Not recommended

Fanttik's X8 APEX + Potent T10 bundle at $179.98. fanttik.com sells the same two units separately for $59.99 and $99.99, $159.98 together, so the bundle costs $20 more.
